260.title: Rock and sand (Matthew 7:24–27)
260.hook: the wise build on rock by doing these words, not just hearing them
260.howItsDone: Many Christians treat this parable as the key to the whole Sermon on the Mount, and children in many churches learn it as a song about the wise man who built his house upon the rock.

segments.voice: Yesterday, by their fruits, and the end of a week. Your line was know it by its fruit. Did someone's actions tell you more than their words? Day two hundred sixty.

You've seen the footage. A storm rolls in, the river rises, and a house that looked perfectly fine yesterday slides sideways into the water. From the street, before the storm, you couldn't have told which houses would stand. Same paint, same windows, same view. The difference was underneath, where nobody looks. For almost three chapters Jesus has been talking on this hillside: blessed are the poor in spirit, love your enemies, the Lord's Prayer, the birds, the lilies, the narrow gate. And now he ends the whole sermon with a story about two builders and one storm. Today, rock and sand.
screen: `THE HOUSE SLIDES INTO THE RIVER.` → `SAME PAINT, SAME WINDOWS.` → `TWO BUILDERS, ONE STORM.`

segments.voice: Here's how it starts, in the King James Bible: "Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock." Notice the two verbs. Hear, and do. Then the storm: "And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock." Now the second builder. Word for word, the storm is the same. Same rain, same floods, same wind. Jesus doesn't promise that the wise builder skips the storm. Both houses get hit. The only difference is what's underneath. And the second one "heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not." That's the whole difference. Not hearing versus not hearing. Both builders heard every word of the sermon. One did it, and one didn't. And the ending is blunt: "and it fell: and great was the fall of it." In that part of the world, there are dry riverbeds that sit flat and sandy most of the year, easy to build on. Then a winter storm comes, and they fill with a rushing flood in an hour. Building on the sand wasn't stupid. It was easy. Rock takes digging. The Greek word for rock is petra, and listeners who know the Gospels will hear an echo later, when Jesus gives Simon the nickname Peter, the rock. The point for an ordinary day is simple and hard. Nobody builds a house by listening to a podcast about houses. The sermon only holds if it's done.
screen: `HEAR, AND DO.` · `THE SAME STORM FOR BOTH.` · `SAND IS EASY; ROCK TAKES DIGGING.` · `PETRA: ROCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Walk back through the sermon in your mind, and pick one thing to actually do today. Maybe give something in secret. Maybe take the plank out first. Maybe watch a bird instead of worrying. Maybe do for someone what you'd want done for you. Choose just one. Picture exactly when and where you'll do it. That's one stone laid on rock. The bell holds the time.
Rock and sand. Two builders heard the same words and faced the same storm. One did what he heard.
Your line: build on rock. Today, do the one thing from the sermon you just chose. Not think about it. Do it. Day two hundred sixty.

myth: the wise builder's house missed the storm
the rain, floods and winds are the same for both. the ground underneath is different.
the foolish builder never heard the sermon
"every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not." he heard every word.
this story ends the Sermon on the Mount
it's the last teaching before the crowds react.

fork.setup: you've heard the whole sermon. the storm is coming. what makes your house stand?
options: a good view and strong paint.
fork.reveal: "whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them" builds on rock. hearing alone is sand.

original.note: Greek: rock, bedrock; the same word echoes when Simon is called Peter.

trapdoor: what you thought: good people don't get hit by storms.
what it means: storms come for everyone; what holds is having done the words, not just heard them.
what a scholar hears: the sermon's closing parable, hear-and-do; dry riverbeds that flood in winter; and petra, echoed in Peter's name.

261.title: The crowds were astonished (Matthew 7:28–29)
261.hook: he taught as one with authority; the sermon has unsettled people for two thousand years
261.howItsDone: Many Christians return to the Sermon on the Mount again and again, reading Matthew 5 to 7 in one sitting, and some traditions shape their whole way of life around it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rock and sand: two builders, one storm. Your line was build on rock. Which piece of the sermon did you actually do? Day two hundred sixty-one.

Think of the last time something you heard stayed with you on the drive home. A speech, a song, a hard conversation. You turned the radio off because you couldn't take in anything else. For thirty days we've sat on this hillside in Galilee. Blessed are the meek. Salt and light. Love your enemies. Give in secret. Our Father. The birds, the lilies, the plank, the narrow gate, the house on the rock. And now the sermon is over. Jesus stops talking. Matthew doesn't tell us what anyone said next. He tells us what they felt. Today, the crowds were astonished.
screen: `THE DRIVE HOME IN SILENCE.` → `THIRTY DAYS ON A HILLSIDE.` → `THE SERMON ENDS.`

segments.voice: Here are the last lines, in the King James Bible: "And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine: For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes." Astonished is a strong word. The Greek means something like struck, knocked out of your ordinary way of thinking. Not impressed. Shaken. Why? Matthew says it was his authority. The Greek is exousia, the right and the power to act. The scribes were the respected teachers of the law, and a careful teacher then often explained scripture by citing the teachers who came before. That's a good and humble way to teach. But on this hillside, Jesus kept saying something different: ye have heard that it was said, "But I say unto you." He spoke as if the words were his to give. That's the first thing that astonished them. The second is the content. Turn the other cheek. Love your enemy. Don't worry. Don't judge. People have been unsettled by this sermon ever since. Some Christians take it very literally, and a few traditions refuse to swear oaths or bear arms because of it. Others read it as the shape of life in God's kingdom, a goal no one reaches alone. In the 1930s, the German pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote a book on it and paid for his convictions with his life. Martin Luther King Jr. drew on its love for enemies in the civil rights movement. What almost nobody has done is read it and feel comfortable. The crowds didn't either. That may be exactly how it was meant to land.
screen: `ASTONISHED: KNOCKED OFF BALANCE.` · `AS ONE HAVING AUTHORITY.` · `BUT I SAY UNTO YOU.` · `UNSETTLED FOR TWO THOUSAND YEARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reread the Beatitudes, the sermon's opening. If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, find Matthew chapter five, verses three to twelve, and read them slowly. If not, just take the first one: "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." Let one line land. Which one pushes on you? Don't argue with it. Just notice where it presses. The bell holds the time.
The crowds were astonished. Knocked off balance by a teacher who spoke with authority, and by what he said.

Your line: let it unsettle you. Today, carry the one line that pressed on you, and don't rush to make it comfortable. That's the end of the Sermon on the Mount. Tomorrow, we walk out into the desert. Day two hundred sixty-one.

fork.reveal: "the people were astonished at his doctrine: For he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes."

original.note: Greek: authority, the right and power to act.

what a scholar hears: exousia against the scribes' way of citing earlier teachers; the 'but I say unto you' pattern; and Matthew's formula, 'when Jesus had ended these sayings', which closes each of his five big teaching blocks.

sources.ref: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Nachfolge (The Cost of Discipleship), 1937

262.title: The desert fathers
262.hook: in the 300s, men like Antony went into the Egyptian desert to pray and people came asking for a word
262.howItsDone: Many Christians, especially in Orthodox and Catholic monastic traditions, still read the Sayings of the Desert Fathers and seek out a spiritual father or mother, an elder, for a word of guidance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crowds were astonished, and the Sermon on the Mount came to an end. Your line was let it unsettle you. Which line is still pressing? Day two hundred sixty-two.

Picture a young man in Egypt, around the year 270. His parents have died and left him land. One Sunday he walks into church and hears the Gospel read, the words Jesus said to a rich young man: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor." He takes it personally. He sells the land, gives the money away, and eventually walks into the desert to pray. His name is Antony. He wanted to be alone with God. What happened instead is that people followed him. Thousands, over the years. And when they found him, they asked for one thing. Today's word: abba.
screen: `EGYPT, AROUND 270.` → `SELL THAT THOU HAST.` → `INTO THE DESERT.` → `PEOPLE FOLLOWED.`

segments.voice: Today we start a new stretch of the path: the mystics, the Christians across the centuries who gave their whole lives to prayer. And they begin in the sand. In the 300s, men and women went out into the deserts of Egypt, Palestine and Syria. Some lived alone in caves. Some lived in loose villages of huts, meeting on Sundays. The desert was not an escape to comfort. It was hot, empty and hungry, and they went on purpose, to strip life down to God and the heart. The name people gave a wise old monk was abba. You've heard that word before on this path. It's the Aramaic word for father, the family word. Jesus prayed it in the garden: "Abba, Father, all things are possible unto thee." In the desert, it became a title of love and respect for a spiritual father. And visitors would walk for days, find an abba sitting outside his hut, and say one simple thing: Abba, give me a word. Not a lecture. A word. One short saying to take home and live on, maybe for years. Those sayings were remembered and written down, and a collection of them, the Sayings of the Desert Fathers, is still read today. They're short, strange and often funny. One tradition tells of Antony seeing the snares of evil spread over the whole earth and asking who could possibly get through them. The answer he heard was a single word: humility. That's the desert in miniature. Not a system. A word, given by someone who had lived it, to someone who had walked a long way to ask.
screen: `A NEW STRETCH: THE MYSTICS.` · `INTO THE DESERT, ON PURPOSE.` · `ABBA: FATHER.` · `GIVE ME A WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of an elder in your life, someone older who has lived through more than you. A grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor, a boss who was kind. Picture sitting with them. If you asked for one word, one short piece of advice, what do you think they'd say? Hold that word. Then, sometime this week, actually ask them. The bell holds the time.
Abba. Father, in Aramaic. The name the desert gave its wise old monks.
Your line: give me a word. Today, ask one older person for one word of advice. Just one. And write down what they say. Day two hundred sixty-two.

what a scholar hears: Athanasius's Life of Antony, and the Apophthegmata Patrum, the sayings collected in Greek in the fifth century.
